title: Speech at home
hook: your best self goes to the group chat; the lady Vedehika was gentle too, until someone pushed
tomorrow: a true thing, said at the wrong moment: is it still right speech?

segments.voice: Yesterday, enough: contentment, the best riches, light as a bird with only its wings. That closed money. Now, the harder currency: words, at home.

The group chat gets the best version: patient, funny, generous with hearts. Then someone at home asks where the charger went, for the third time, and a voice comes out that nobody online has ever heard. Same person, same afternoon, two completely different people. Why is kindness hardest with the people you live with? The Buddha told a story about exactly that, starring a woman everyone called gentle.
screen: `THE GROUP CHAT GETS THE BEST VERSION.` → `HOME GETS THE OTHER VOICE.` → `A WOMAN EVERYONE CALLED GENTLE.`

segments.voice: In the city of Savatthi lived the lady Vedehika, known all over the neighborhood as calm, gentle, peaceful. Her maid Kali, a good worker, wondered: is she really, or has nobody ever pushed her? So one morning Kali got up late. Hey, Kali! Yes, madam? Why so late? Oh, no reason. Vedehika frowned. The next day Kali slept later, and Vedehika snapped. On the third day, later still, Vedehika lost her temper and struck her with the pin from the door. Kali ran out to the neighbors, and by evening the gentle lady's name had flipped. The Buddha's point is uncomfortable: a person is only as gentle as the first time disagreeable words touch them. Then he names five ways anyone may speak to us: at the right time or not, true or not, gentle or harsh, helpful or not, with goodwill or with hate. Any of the five can come. The training is to keep the mind unchanged, let no harsh words out, and stay with goodwill toward the one speaking. Home is where all five arrive, early and late, from people who know exactly where it hurts. There's no audience to perform for, no reputation to protect, and nobody leaves when the conversation goes badly. That's why it's hardest there. And it's also why a family can tell, better than any neighbor, whether the gentleness is real. The Buddha doesn't ask anyone to pretend nothing stings. He asks that the sting not get the last word.
screen: `THE LADY VEDEHIKA, KNOWN AS GENTLE.` · `KALI GETS UP LATE, THREE TIMES.` · `FIVE WAYS ANYONE MAY SPEAK.` · `MIND UNCHANGED, NO HARSH WORDS.` · then, large: `KIND AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Say one plain, kind sentence out loud, softly, the kind you could say at home today: thanks for dinner, or, I'm glad you're here. Say it twice, slowly. Then sit with how it feels in your mouth, and who it was for. If nothing comes, the plainest sentence works too: good night, sleep well.
Speech at home: right speech where it's tested, with people who can push every button. Gentle counts most when pushed.
Your line: kind at home, the place it's hardest. One of four, on speech at home.

screen: `DAY 1587 COUNTS.` → `SPEECH AT HOME · 1 OF 4.` → `TOMORROW: A TRUE THING AT THE WRONG MOMENT?`

howItsDone: Right speech is one step of the eightfold path; Buddhist teachers often point lay students to MN 21's five ways of speaking when they talk about patience with family.

fork.setup: your sister snaps at you before school for using all the hot water. you're tired and she's not wrong. what does the Buddha's training ask you to keep?
options: an honest, sharp reply, because true speech matters more than gentle speech.
a mind unchanged, no harsh words back, and goodwill toward her.
a calm face on the outside, while you hold the grudge for later.
fork.reveal: MN 21's training is to keep the mind unchanged, let no harsh words out, and stay with goodwill, whichever way someone speaks.

original.note: Pali: right speech, one step of the eightfold path.

trapdoor: what you thought: right speech means being polite.
what it means: gentleness is only tested when someone pushes, and home is where people push hardest; the training is goodwill under pressure.
what a scholar hears: MN 21, the Kakacupama Sutta, tells of Vedehika and her maid Kali, then lists five ways others may speak to us and the training to keep the mind unchanged.
guess: right speech with family, where it's tested most
speaking only your family's home language
a rule of silence kept inside a monastery

chat.says: mom saw the tablet in my cart and gave a speech. i said 'my money, not yours.' she went silent.
options: Gentle counts most when you're pushed. Go back with no harsh words, just goodwill.
She pushed first, so it's on her. Kindness only owes kindness back.
Say nothing for a few days. Silence keeps the peace better than words.
chat.meaning: In MN 21, Vedehika's gentleness lasted only until she was pushed. The training is no harsh words and goodwill, whoever spoke first.

tie.story: The lady Vedehika was called gentle until her maid pushed her, and then she snapped and struck.
tie.friend: Mai got pushed and snapped too; she can go back to her mom with no harsh words and goodwill.
tie.you: who at home gets the voice nobody else hears?

Savatthi.meaning: a city where the Buddha stayed and taught

Vedehika.meaning: a housewife in the Buddha's story, famed for being gentle

Kali.meaning: Vedehika's maid, who tested her calm

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 21 (Kakacupama Sutta: the lady Vedehika of Savatthi and her maid Kali; the five ways others may speak; the training to keep the mind unaffected, utter no evil words, and abide with goodwill)

notes: MN 21's Vedehika story paraphrased and shortened (in the sutta Vedehika strikes Kali on the head with a door pin and breaks her head; the script says 'struck her with the pin from the door'). Mild violence: a gentle note for parents if needed.
Five ways of speech (timely/untimely, true/untrue, gentle/harsh, beneficial/not, with goodwill/with hate) paraphrased; confirm.
The saw simile from MN 21 is deliberately left out (heavier image; may suit a later day).
Life shape: the chat leads. The practice ('say one kind sentence out loud') offers example sentences, not a prayer.
games.gloss: Kali's Pali spelling (Kāḷī) uses the retroflex ḷ; script left out rather than guessed.
